reconstructed_theorem_text:
For every natural number d with d ≥ 2, every real number κ with κ ≥ 2, and every natural number n with 1 ≤ n < d and √κ ≤ (d viewed as a real number) − (n viewed as a real number), define, for each coordinate index i = 0, …, d−1,
  θ_i = (i + 1/2)π/d,
  λ_i = (κ + 1)/2 + ((κ − 1)/2) cos(θ_i),
and let Λ = diag(λ_0, …, λ_{d−1}). Let μ be the centered Gaussian probability measure on the standard Euclidean space R^d with covariance matrix Λ^{-1}. Thus Λ is the precision matrix, and the covariance of coordinate i is 1/λ_i; on the stated parameter range all λ_i are positive.
For x = (x_0, …, x_{d−1}), let
  Q(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{d−1} cos(n θ_i) x_i^2,
  M = ∫_{R^d} ||x||_2^2 dμ(x),
  b = ∫_{R^d} Q(x) dμ(x).
These are integrals over the entire Euclidean space against that same probability measure. Then all four assertions hold simultaneously:
  M > 0;
  (−1)^n b > 0;
  (1 − exp(−4)) exp(−3n/√κ) ≤ |b|/M;
  |b|/M ≤ exp(−2n/√κ).
In particular, the sign assertion says that b is positive when n is even and negative when n is odd. The displayed estimates use the absolute value of b and normalize it by the full expected squared Euclidean norm M, with no division of M by d.
objects: The finite coordinate set is Fin d, identified with i = 0,…,d−1. The coordinate angles are θ_i = ((i as a real)+1/2)π/(d as a real); the real eigenvalues are λ_i = (κ+1)/2 + ((κ−1)/2)cos θ_i. Λ is their real d-by-d diagonal matrix. μ is multivariateGaussian with mean the zero vector and second argument Λ^{-1}. Q is the diagonal quadratic polynomial Σ_i cos((n as a real)θ_i)x_i². M is ∫||x||₂² dμ and b is ∫Q(x)dμ, both real scalars.
domains: d and n belong to ℕ. κ belongs to ℝ. Each index i belongs to Fin d. Points x belong to EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), identified with ℝ^d with its standard Euclidean norm and Lebesgue coordinates. θ_i, λ_i, Q(x), M, b and the final ratio are real. Λ is a matrix in Matrix (Fin d) (Fin d) ℝ, and μ is a measure on this Euclidean space. The Gaussian is a probability measure in the stated positive definite regime.

Equivalently it asserts the conclusion for every admissible triple (d,κ,n). Every θ, λ, Λ, μ, Q, M and b is a locally let-defined function of this triple, not an existential choice or an additional universal parameter. The local coordinate i and integration variable x are bound only inside their definitions. The proof witnesses impose hypotheses and do not change the defined numerical objects.

The last subtraction is real subtraction of the two explicitly cast naturals. There is no additional assumed integrability statement, arbitrary covariance choice, arbitrary test matrix, arbitrary vector, asymptotic limit, or further condition on n. Positivity and well-posedness of the Gaussian and integrals are consequences of these definitions and admissible parameters, rather than extra hypotheses.
conclusion: A four-way conjunction: (1) 0<M; (2) 0<(−1:ℝ)^n b; (3) (1−exp(−4))exp(−3(n:ℝ)/√κ)≤|b|/M; and (4) |b|/M≤exp(−2(n:ℝ)/√κ). The sign inequality is strict and uses the natural exponent n, so b>0 for even n and b<0 for odd n. Both ratio bounds are non-strict, involve |b|, and apply for every admissible finite triple. No equality, limiting rate, optimality, or extension beyond the stated parameter set is asserted.

The two integrals use the same centered Gaussian μ on all of ℝ^d. The second argument of multivariateGaussian is covariance on the positive semidefinite domain: here it is Λ^{-1}, while Λ itself is precision. The approved totalized Gaussian square root and the totalized inverse and integral conventions must be read literally, but the stated domain is positive definite and integrable. The exponent n in (−1)^n is a natural power; the powers x_i² and ||x||² are natural squares. n in the cosine and exponential expressions is cast to ℝ. The square root is the nonnegative real square root. Absolute value applies to b, and the ratio denominator is M. There is no natural subtraction in this statement, including in the displayed gap condition.
